strengths: Although no contribution type is declared, the paper is best assessed as Applied/Systems: its main value is an engineered, modular 3D Gaussian Splatting training framework rather than a new reconstruction model. Under that lens, the reported end-to-end efficiency gains are potentially useful to the vision community.

The paper identifies concrete GPU bottlenecks in 3DGS, including global-memory atomic contention, degraded spatial locality, warp divergence, loose 2D bounds, and wasted fragment processing. The profiling observations provide plausible motivation for the proposed optimizations.

LiteGS combines several practically relevant techniques: Morton-order clustering, cluster-level culling and compaction, sparse gradients, fused optimization, tighter AABBs, smaller tiles, and shared-memory gradient reduction.

The reported runtime improvements are substantial and consistent across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes and two GPUs: approximately 3.4x over the original implementation and 1.4x over the TamingGS-enhanced baseline. PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS remain broadly comparable or improve slightly.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is inadequate for the breadth of the claims. There are no component ablations, so the contributions of clustering, compaction, sparse gradients, fused Adam, tighter AABBs, 8x8 tiles, and multi-batch reduction cannot be separated. Intermediate statistics such as cache-hit rate and patch count do not establish their effects on end-to-end runtime or quality.

The claimed approximately 30% reduction in GPU memory is not supported by any table, measurement protocol, or discussion. Likewise, claims of better usability, rapid prototyping, and production readiness receive no quantitative or qualitative evaluation.

The comparison is too narrow for an Applied/Systems paper. Despite discussing gsplat and DistWar, the experiments only compare against original 3DGS and a TamingGS-integrated variant. Training is evaluated on one dataset, with no tests of other scene scales, Gaussian counts, image resolutions, or GPU architectures beyond A100 and RTX 3090.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript says that source code is available but leaves the location blank. It omits important implementation details, exact density-control changes, timing methodology, warm-up and repetition protocol, software versions, memory measurements, and sufficiently precise descriptions or formulas for the tighter AABB and reduction implementations.

The fairness of the quality and timing comparisons is unclear. The method changes the frequency and magnitude of density-control operations, while the paper also reports unspecified SfM processing and parameter adjustments. These changes could alter Gaussian counts, workload, convergence, and quality, yet final point counts and per-iteration or time-to-quality curves are absent.

The technical exposition is incomplete. The reduction algorithms are only high-level pseudocode, numerical equivalence and gradient correctness are not validated, and the consequences of compacting or reordering optimizer state are not explained. The framework is also not fully script-customizable because rasterization remains CUDA-only.

The manuscript is not publication-ready: Figure 1 has a placeholder caption, several plots lack sufficient methodological context, no visual reconstruction results are shown, and frequent grammatical and typographical errors impair clarity. Overall, the promising speed results do not yet form a sufficiently rigorous and reproducible systems contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: reducing the substantial training cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting while improving implementation modularity. Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General because its main contribution is an optimized framework; this makes system design, benchmarking rigor, and reproducibility central to the assessment.

The optimizations are motivated by plausible profiling observations, including atomic-operation contention, poor spatial locality, warp divergence, and redundant rasterization. Morton ordering, cluster-based culling and compaction, tighter 2D bounds, smaller tiles, fused optimization, and shared-memory reduction form a reasonably coherent engineering package.

The reported end-to-end improvements are substantial and consistent across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes: approximately 3.4x over the stated 3DGS baseline and 1.4x over the TamingGS-enhanced baseline. Evaluation on both A100 and RTX 3090 GPUs provides some evidence that the gains are not confined to one architecture.
The reported PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS results remain comparable to or modestly better than 3DGS, suggesting that the acceleration is not obtained through an obvious loss of rendering quality.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence is inadequate for a systems paper with many interacting optimizations. There is no component-wise ablation of clustering, compaction, sparse gradients, fused Adam, tighter AABBs, 8x8 tiles, or multi-batch reduction. Consequently, the reader cannot determine which components produce the speedup, whether some are redundant, or what their individual quality and memory costs are.

The headline claim of approximately 30% lower GPU memory usage is not supported by any reported memory measurements, protocol, table, or figure. Likewise, the claimed usability and rapid-prototyping advantages of the modular APIs receive no quantitative or qualitative evaluation, such as implementation case studies, code-size comparisons, or examples of adding a new rendering feature.

Reproducibility is poor. The manuscript says that full source code is available, but the corresponding location is blank and the PDF contains no code link. It also omits important implementation and benchmarking details, including software versions, exact training configurations, iteration counts, timing boundaries, run counts or variability, peak-GPU-memory methodology, and several modified density-management parameters.

The comparison is not demonstrably controlled. LiteGS changes the frequency and scale of density-control operations, but the exact settings and resulting Gaussian counts are not reported; these changes can directly affect both runtime and quality. The paper also mentions unspecified SfM processing and parameter adjustments. Without reporting workloads, Gaussian trajectories, or tightly matched configurations, the end-to-end speed differences cannot be attributed solely to the proposed implementation.

The technical presentation is too incomplete to validate the implementation. The tighter AABB construction is not derived, the cluster/AABB update and sorting costs are not characterized, and the reduction algorithms are only high-level pseudocode with unclear initialization, synchronization, numerical behavior, and resource requirements. There is no gradient-correctness or numerical-equivalence test against the reference rasterizer.

Evaluation is restricted to one dataset and only end-to-end time and image-quality metrics. There are no kernel-level timings, throughput measurements, memory results, scalability analyses over resolution or Gaussian count, costs of re-clustering, or comparisons with the most directly relevant modular library, gsplat. Figure 1 instead makes unsupported qualitative placements of competing methods.

The manuscript is not publication-ready in clarity or scholarship. It contains numerous grammatical errors and malformed spacing, inconsistent terminology and capitalization, an unfinished Figure 1 caption ('...'), and imprecise claims such as 'superiority.' Related-work coverage ends largely in 2024 and does not clearly distinguish which optimization ideas are genuinely new from those adopted from TamingGS, standard GPU techniques, or prior differentiable-rasterization work. Overall, the promising speed numbers are insufficiently substantiated, so important concerns favor rejection.

The reported end-to-end speedups are substantial and consistent across all nine Mip-NeRF 360 scenes: roughly 3.4x over the original 3DGS implementation and 1.4x over the TamingGS-integrated version.
Evaluation on both A100 and RTX 3090 GPUs provides useful evidence that the performance gains are not confined to one accelerator generation.

LiteGS attacks several credible systems bottlenecks—global atomic contention during backward rasterization, poor spatial locality after density control, overly coarse Gaussian bounds, and unnecessary fragment processing—rather than relying on a single narrow optimization.

The combination of Morton-ordered clustering, cluster culling and compaction, tighter 2D AABBs, 8x8 tiles, fused optimization, and shared-memory gradient reduction is technically sensible and practically motivated by profiling observations.

The PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS results indicate that the large training-time improvements do not degrade novel-view synthesis quality; results are generally slightly better than the reported 3DGS baseline.
Offering modular operators and both script/autograd-oriented and CUDA-oriented interfaces could make the framework useful for both research prototyping and performance-sensitive deployment.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence does not isolate the contributions of the many proposed optimizations. Component-wise ablations should report end-to-end time, per-stage time, memory, and reconstruction quality for clustering/compaction, sparse gradients, fused Adam, tighter AABBs, tile size, and multi-batch reduction. Without these, it is difficult to validate the causal claims or understand the speed–accuracy trade-offs.
The abstract claims approximately 30% lower GPU memory usage, but the evaluation contains no memory measurements. This central quantitative claim is therefore unsupported.

The comparison set is too narrow for a framework paper. Although gsplat is identified as the closest modular library and appears in Figure 1, it is not evaluated for speed, memory, output quality, API coverage, or customization effort. The paper also lacks direct experimental comparison to other relevant acceleration work such as DISTWAR.

Reproducibility is presently weak: the sentence claiming that source code is available contains no URL, while important implementation and measurement details are absent, including software versions, timing protocol and synchronization, number of runs or variance, exact training configuration, Gaussian counts, peak-memory methodology, and precise parameter changes.

The claim of comparison under identical training parameters is complicated by the stated changes to density-management frequency and scale. The paper should quantify whether LiteGS performs the same optimization work and ends with comparable Gaussian counts. Similarly, the special SfM/COLMAP adjustments are not specified clearly enough to establish a fully controlled comparison.

Evaluation is confined to one dataset. For a general-purpose framework, evidence on additional scene types, resolutions, camera distributions, and larger scenes would better establish robustness and clarify when cluster culling, compacting, and 8x8 tiling help or hurt.

Several central techniques are insufficiently specified for independent reproduction. In particular, the tighter AABB construction is not derived, cluster rebuilding and ordering behavior are underspecified, and the reduction pseudocode omits important implementation details and contains ambiguous notation.

The modularity and usability claims receive no empirical support. Examples of implementing representative 3DGS extensions, code-size comparisons, or developer-effort measurements would substantiate the claimed research-productivity benefit.

Presentation needs substantial polishing: Figure 1 has the placeholder caption “...”; numerous grammatical and typographical errors remain; some figures lack precise experimental context; and the paper does not include a clear conclusion or limitations discussion. These issues reduce clarity but do not negate the promising systems result.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical bottleneck in 3D Gaussian Splatting and proposes a coherent cross-layer framework combining GPU rasterization, spatial data management, and densification improvements.

Although no contribution type is declared, the work is best assessed as Applied/Systems rather than Algorithms/General. Under that framing, the end-to-end engineering integration and reported speed-quality trade-offs are potentially significant contributions.

The reported results on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending are strong: LiteGS-turbo substantially reduces training time, while LiteGS-balance and LiteGS-quality are competitive with or better than several recent methods in reconstruction quality.

The operator-level rasterization timings and component ablations provide useful evidence beyond a single end-to-end comparison. The proposed one-warp-per-tile design and inexpensive collection of opacity-gradient statistics are particularly interesting.
The manuscript is generally organized around clearly identified bottlenecks, and the intuition for opacity-gradient variance as a densification signal is understandable.
weaknesses: The systems evidence is not yet sufficient for the breadth of the claims. All experiments use only an RTX 3090, despite reliance on architecture-specific register behavior, FP16/half2 operations, and integer warp-reduction instructions. Results across at least two GPU generations, together with peak memory, occupancy, register-spill, cache-miss, sorting overhead, and culling-rate measurements, are needed to establish robustness and explain the speedups.

Several implementation details essential for reproducibility are missing: densification thresholds and split/clone rules, the settings distinguishing turbo/balance/quality, the precise epoch-to-iteration mapping, timing protocol and number of runs, baseline implementations/configurations, and treatment of optimizer state during primitive reordering. The paper claims that the framework is open-sourced but provides no identifiable repository or artifact.

The Cluster-Cull-Compact description raises a correctness concern. It appears to construct cluster AABBs from Gaussian centers without explaining how Gaussian spatial extent and anisotropy are incorporated. Center-only bounds can cull Gaussians whose centers lie outside the frustum but whose support remains visible. The paper provides neither a conservative-bound derivation nor worst-case/scene-level error analysis.

The mixed-precision rasterizer lacks numerical validation. Iterative FP16 transmittance and low-precision color/opacity gradients could accumulate substantial errors for long overlap sequences. No comparison against an FP32 reference, gradient-error measurement, convergence study, or difficult high-overdraw test is supplied.

The ablations do not cleanly isolate the proposed components. Table 2 principally toggles culling and does not separately assess Morton sorting, clustering, compaction, or sparse cluster updates. Table 4 changes both the opacity policy and associated hyperparameters, while replacing variance with a per-pixel-error method rather than comparing directly with the original positional-gradient criterion. Scanline and mixed-precision contributions are not separately quantified.

Some technical presentation is insufficiently precise. Equations use the covariance where the inverse covariance/conic would normally appear; Algorithm 1 introduces an undefined variable d in quad = -0.5d; and the scanline direction and coefficient derivation are not specified clearly enough to verify correctness.

The empirical presentation contains inconsistencies and overstatements. Table 3 shows the proposed backward rasterizer losing to the tensor-core method at 500K primitives, contradicting the claim that it outperforms it across all scales. The Tanks & Temples 30K result in Table 1's note reports SSIM 0.780, whereas Table 2 reports 0.870, and the claimed 0.2–0.4 dB advantage over 3DGS-MCMC does not match all table differences. Claims of universally dominant or Pareto-optimal performance also overlook cases where LiteGS-turbo has worse SSIM/LPIPS.

There are no qualitative reconstruction comparisons, per-scene results, variance across runs, or analysis of failure cases. Dataset-level averages alone make it difficult to determine whether the new densification criterion consistently improves geometry or hides regressions on particular scenes. Overall, the ideas and headline results are promising, but the correctness, reproducibility, and hardware-generalization gaps leave a slight preference for rejection in the current form.

strengths: Best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution rather than a purely algorithmic paper. The combination of GPU-kernel design, spatial data management, and densification is relevant to an important 3D vision workload.

The reported efficiency gains are potentially significant: LiteGS presents favorable speed-quality trade-offs on Mip-NeRF 360, Tanks & Temples, and Deep Blending, including large improvements over the original 3DGS implementation.

The paper identifies plausible bottlenecks and proposes reasonably motivated remedies: one-warp-per-tile reduction, scanline reuse, Morton-ordered cluster culling/compaction, and opacity-gradient variance for densification.
The evaluation covers three standard datasets, multiple model-size regimes, image-quality metrics, primitive counts, end-to-end training time, and rasterizer microbenchmarks.
The manuscript is organized around a coherent systems narrative, and it acknowledges limitations of center-based Morton sorting.
weaknesses: The experimental evidence does not adequately substantiate the strong systems claims. Results are only dataset averages, with no per-scene results, run-to-run variation, timing protocol, warm-up/synchronization details, peak memory measurements, or evidence that every baseline was executed under identical software and hardware conditions. This is especially consequential for claimed speedups as high as 13.4x.

The ablations do not isolate the proposed components. Table 2 disables the overall culling pipeline but does not separate sorting, clustering, culling, and compaction. Table 3 tests only one scene and three primitive counts, without end-to-end incremental ablations or profiling evidence for the claimed reductions in atomic contention, cache misses, divergence, register pressure, and occupancy.

The densification study is confounded. Removing variance substitutes a different error-based method rather than the original 3DGS criterion, while removing decay also changes reset behavior and associated hyperparameters. Consequently, Table 4 does not establish that opacity-gradient variance itself is superior under controlled conditions. Its full-model numbers also do not clearly correspond to any Table 1 configuration.

Several technical descriptions appear inconsistent or erroneous. Equation 2 uses the covariance rather than its inverse in the Gaussian exponent; Algorithm 1 introduces an undefined variable d and gives coefficients whose signs/factors are not clearly consistent with the stated quadratic expansion. The Morton-code section says that three 22-bit coordinates form a 64-bit code, which requires 66 bits, while its summation spans only 21 bits per coordinate. These issues materially undermine confidence in reproducibility and correctness.

The mixed-precision design lacks numerical analysis. Iterative FP16 transmittance accumulation can underflow or accumulate substantial error, yet no accuracy comparison against FP32, error bound, failure analysis, or scene-complexity stress test is provided. The custom integerized floating-point reduction is also described too briefly to assess overflow, rounding, handling of signs and exceptional values, or determinism.

The proposed cluster AABB construction is underspecified: it is unclear whether bounds include each anisotropic Gaussian's spatial support or only its center. Center-only bounds could incorrectly reject visible splats. Sorting frequency, coordinate normalization under outliers, compaction overhead, and interactions with primitive motion/densification are likewise insufficiently documented.

Claims such as “dominant and Pareto-optimal,” “new accuracy record,” and superiority to “virtually all existing solutions” overstate the evidence. LiteGS-turbo is worse than some baselines on SSIM/LPIPS, and the benchmark set omits broader recent alternatives and cross-hardware validation.

Reproducibility is weak despite the claim that the framework is open-sourced: the manuscript supplies no repository identifier, detailed kernel configuration, thresholds for variance-based densification, complete hyperparameters, software versions, or enough implementation detail to reproduce the reported system behavior.

The paper provides almost no qualitative reconstruction results or failure cases. Aggregate PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS cannot show whether mixed precision, aggressive culling, or the new densification rule introduces localized artifacts, thin-structure loss, or view-dependent failures. Overall, the ideas are promising, but the technical inconsistencies and insufficiently controlled systems evaluation currently favor rejection.

strengths: Best assessed as an Applied/Systems contribution: LiteGS combines GPU rasterization, spatial data management, and densification changes into a coherent end-to-end 3DGS training framework. This framing makes the integrated speed-quality improvement more important than novelty of every individual technique.
The reported efficiency gains are substantial: up to 13.4x over original 3DGS, competitive quality in the lightweight setting, and 3.8x-7x faster training than 3DGS-MCMC in the high-quality setting.

Evaluation covers three established datasets, multiple model budgets, several recent baselines, standard reconstruction metrics, primitive counts, end-to-end time, and operator-level timing. The resulting speed-quality trade-offs are generally compelling.

The ablations provide useful evidence for each major component: cluster culling materially reduces training time, while opacity decay and gradient-variance densification consistently improve PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS.

The opacity-gradient-variance criterion has an intuitive motivation: disagreement among pixel-level opacity gradients can indicate that one primitive is insufficient. Its efficient integration with the rasterizer is a particularly appealing codesign aspect.
weaknesses: The hardware evidence is narrow for a systems paper. All experiments use one RTX 3090, yet the paper makes broad claims about Ampere-and-newer GPUs, register configurations, and possible RTX 5090 performance. Results across at least two architectures, together with peak memory and sorting/compaction overheads, are needed to establish portability.

The mixed-precision and integer-mantissa reductions lack numerical validation. The paper reports speed and final image metrics but no forward-error, gradient-error, overflow analysis, or convergence comparison against an FP32 reference. This is important because FP16 transmittance accumulation can underflow or alter gradients.

Reproducibility details are insufficient despite the open-source claim: the manuscript does not specify densification thresholds, how opacity-gradient moments are accumulated across views or iterations, cluster-update costs, baseline execution methodology, or whether all timing numbers were reproduced on identical hardware and software.

Several technical descriptions contain consequential ambiguities or apparent errors. Algorithm 1 uses an undefined variable d in quad=-0.5d and leaves the scanline sign convention unclear. The Morton-code section says coordinates use 22 bits each, which requires 66 bits, while its equation iterates over only 21 bits. The Gaussian equation also calls Sigma a covariance while using it directly rather than its inverse/conic form.

Cluster AABBs appear to be constructed from Gaussian centers without accounting for primitive extent or anisotropy. This is not conservative and can cull Gaussians whose centers lie outside the frustum while their support overlaps it; the aggregate quality ablation does not characterize such errors or difficult cases.

The empirical presentation lacks qualitative render comparisons, per-scene results, repeated-run variability, and a full factorial systems ablation separating scanline evaluation, FP16, integer reduction, Morton sorting, compaction, and sparse updates. Consequently, it is difficult to determine which optimizations drive the gains or whether improvements are consistent across scenes.
